label: GPT-6.1 Sol
output:
Peter, I agree with you about the risks of an informal scheme. Your nine years in payroll are not something I would dismiss, especially on recoveries when people leave and the amount of time these requests can swallow. If the system is “come to HR, explain your problem and we will see”, it is difficult for Finance to forecast and difficult for HR to administer fairly.

Where I disagree quite strongly is with “it’s painful for one or two pay cycles and then people adjust”. We tried closing the window in 2025, for almost exactly the reasons you have given. We ended up reopening it.

Brenda, this is one company’s experience, not a guarantee that yours would be the same. But it may give you something useful to take into the meeting on the 18th.

We have about 340 staff in logistics, mainly drivers, turn-boys, loaders and warehouse clerks. We stopped salary advances in February 2025 after Finance pushed back. We gave two months’ notice rather than the three you recommend, Peter, and arranged a financial literacy session with the SACCO. We did not simply announce it on a Friday and leave people to manage on Monday.

The need for money did not disappear. What changed was where people went for it, and where the consequences showed up.

**In the six months after we closed the scheme, reception logged 61 debt-collector or loan-app calls to the office.** Previously it had been a handful. Some apps were also calling supervisors whom employees had listed as “referees”.

Those were employees’ own borrowing decisions and contracts, as you say. But the calls were coming to our reception and our supervisors. The company was outside the lending arrangement, but it was not outside the consequences.

We also saw unplanned absence rise on the two days after month-end. Our Fleet Manager linked at least three missed Mombasa runs to drivers being away “sorting out” loans. I would not claim every absence was caused by stopping advances, or that those three runs prove the whole case on their own. But neither could we honestly say that people had adjusted after a couple of payrolls and the matter was behind us.

One loader at Changamwe had six loan apps running at once by the time he came to me. He was borrowing from one to pay another. It took us four months, working with payroll, to unwind it. That was considerably more HR work than processing an advance under a clear policy would have been.

I mention him because “their own contract” is legally one thing; what lands in your office is another. We still had the distressed employee, the payroll discussions and the time spent resolving the problem. We had removed the advance, not the work.

On the SACCO point, I am a supporter. We involved ours when we closed the scheme, and I would still encourage staff to use it. But our SACCO loans take two to three weeks to process and require guarantors. That is not a workable answer to a child being sent home from school over fees on a Tuesday.

Financial literacy is useful too. It should be part of the support, but we have to be realistic about what it can solve. On KES 28,000 a month, understanding a budget does not necessarily mean there is enough room in it to absorb an emergency. There are poor borrowing decisions, certainly. There are also people whose immediate problem is that the money is needed today and payday is not today.

**We reopened advances in September 2025, but we did not reopen the old informal arrangement.** That distinction is important. The choice was not between letting HR hand out money without limits and stopping altogether.

Our written policy now has these basic rules:

- A maximum advance of **40% of net pay**.
- No more than one advance per pay cycle.
- Full repayment at the next payroll.
- No fee.
- Requests through the payroll portal, rather than a queue at my office.
- A check on existing deductions before approval.

The 40% is a ceiling, not an automatic entitlement regardless of other commitments. We also check the Employment Act’s limit on total deductions of two-thirds of wages before approving anything. Nobody should be left with nothing at month-end because we approved an advance without looking at the rest of their payroll position.

Since reopening, we have been handling roughly 55–70 requests a month, with the average around KES 9,000. We have recovered everything apart from balances owed by two leavers. The total written off was roughly KES 14,000 for the year.

That is not zero risk, Peter, and your warning about leavers is fair. We have actual losses to show for it. But we can now discuss the size of that risk rather than treating any possible loss as a reason to stop.

The same applies to administration. There is work involved. A portal does not make payroll checks or reconciliation happen by magic. What it does is remove much of the personal pleading and case-by-case negotiation from my office. Staff know the rules and the route. Payroll has something consistent to administer.

Our Finance Manager now defends the scheme himself. The forecast impact is known in advance because there is a fixed ceiling, rather than an open-ended informal commitment. He has not suddenly decided we should become a bank. He has decided that a controlled arrangement is more manageable than the alternative we experienced.

I also think we need to compare the costs fairly. Advance administration and write-offs are visible in Finance and payroll. Reception answering collection calls, supervisors dealing with “referee” calls, HR helping untangle debts, absence and missed runs sit across several departments. They are easier to overlook, not necessarily smaller.

I cannot put a defensible shilling figure on every one of those consequences, so I would not manufacture a neat return-on-investment calculation. But comparing the cost of advances with an assumed cost of zero after closure gave us the wrong picture.

Brenda, for the 18th, I would acknowledge the Finance Manager’s strongest point straight away: an unwritten scheme with no clear limit is not a good arrangement. You do not need to defend that in order to oppose a blanket shutdown.

I would take a one-page policy proposal with a cap, frequency limit, repayment rule and approval route. Ours is 40% of net pay, once per cycle, recovered at the next payroll, through the portal with deduction checks. Your Finance Manager may want a different cap. That is a much more useful discussion than whether HR is being sympathetic and Finance is being hard-hearted.

Then take whatever numbers you can get from your own payroll: monthly requests, average and total amounts advanced, repeat users, outstanding balances, leaver losses and time spent administering it. Ask Finance to help establish the maximum cash exposure under the proposed rules. If necessary, suggest a time-limited trial with an agreed review.

Our 61 calls and KES 14,000 write-off are our figures, not yours. They are a reason to examine the alternative, not numbers to put into your own forecast.

Peter, I think you are right that repeated advances can indicate a deeper problem, and that HR should not become an unrestricted lender. Where our experience differs is the assumption that withdrawing the facility resolves that problem. For us, it moved it into more expensive and disruptive places.

What worked was not keeping the old scheme. It was replacing it with rules.
